expansionNote: Authored from scratch using NCERT Ganita Prakash Class 8 Ch.1 'A Square and A Cube' (current edition) plus the prior edition's Ch.5/Ch.6 as supplementary source. 40 questions across 11 learning objectives, mixed Understand/Apply/Reason/Challenge progression per section: conceptual/definitional recall, direct prime-factorisation application, multi-step reasoning (Pythagorean triplet construction, smallest-multiplier/divisor problems), and real-world area/volume word problems. Difficulty split: 15 Easy (37.5%), 16 Medium (40%), 9 Hard (22.5%) — matches the style already used for Understanding Quadrilaterals. Every expectedAnswer is a single short value (a number, a short phrase, or Yes/No/True/False) deliberately, to stay reliably compatible with the current exact-string-match evaluator — no open-ended 'explain your reasoning' questions were included, unlike some other chapters, specifically to avoid the known evaluator brittleness documented in those chapters' answer-keys.json.

The legacy `objective` field is retired and does not appear on any question below. See docs/Structured-Learning-Content-Design-Proposal.md §I.
importNote: 12 questions (sc-q41-sc-q52) added 2026-08-19, sourced from a third-party school assessment (Orchids The International School, Weekly Test 8 / Capstone Assessment, Term 1 2026-27) rather than the NCERT source documents already cited above - sourceRef is null throughout, matching the author-original convention Linear Equations already established for le-q21-44. Selected only content genuinely suited to this chapter's four existing question types (short_text/numeric/single_choice/multi_choice); one source question (a matching-the-following activity pairing 4,100², 22²-21², sqrt(676) and 5² to their results/properties) used a question format this project has not implemented (matching) and was decomposed into 4 independent questions (sc-q44-sc-q47) rather than imported verbatim or forcing a new type - see each question's own content for the preserved mathematical relationship. One duplicate candidate (a source question asking for 6 cubed) was dropped entirely: sc-q25 already asks this verbatim. Two source answers were independently re-derived rather than trusted as-authored, since the source paper's own handwritten work was mathematically inconsistent with the printed question: the 'greater than 15,000' comparison (sc-q43 - correct answer is Platform 2 only, verified by direct computation) and the matching activity's own answer key (verified pairing: 4,100^2 ends in 4 zeros, 22^2-21^2=43, sqrt(676)=26, 5^2=1+3+5+7+9 - the source paper's handwritten matching did not agree with this and was not used). objectiveIds are set only where an existing learning objective in canonical-topic.json genuinely fits (obj-squares-odd-sum, obj-cubes-smallest-multiplier, obj-squares-pythagorean-triplet - clean matches; obj-square-roots-prime-factorisation and obj-cubes-prime-factorisation - following this chapter's own established loose-filing precedent for plain computation, e.g. sc-q01/sc-q24/sc-q25) and left unset for three genuinely novel techniques this chapter's 11 objectives don't yet name (identity-based squaring, difference-of-squares, place-value/trailing-zero reasoning) rather than mis-filed or invented - a real, flagged content gap, not an oversight.
secondExpansionNote: 8 questions (sc-q53-sc-q60) added 2026-09-02 for the Content Expansion for Exam Practice milestone, bringing this chapter to the ~60-question target. Targeted the weakest-covered objectives identified by inventory: obj-squares-between-squares and obj-square-roots-estimation/repeated-subtraction each had only 1 question across the existing 52; this batch adds one more to obj-squares-between-squares, one more to obj-square-roots-repeated-subtraction, and two more to obj-square-roots-estimation, plus one each to obj-squares-pythagorean-triplet, obj-cube-roots-prime-factorisation, obj-cubes-smallest-multiplier and obj-squares-unit-digit for difficulty balance. All 8 are original numbers/scenarios, checked against the existing 52 for duplication. New difficulty split: 3 Easy, 3 Medium, 2 Hard, bringing the chapter total to 23 Easy / 25 Medium / 12 Hard (60 total).

questions.prompt: What is 15 squared (15²)?
hints: Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself.
Compute 15 × 15.

questions.prompt: Is 250 a perfect square?
hints: Think of the two consecutive whole numbers whose squares are just below and just above 250.
15² = 225 and 16² = 256 — does 250 fall exactly on either one?

questions.prompt: True or False: a number ending in 3 can never be a perfect square.
hints: Recall which unit's digits are possible for a perfect square.
Perfect squares only ever end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: False, because some other digits like 2 or 7 also seem excluded so the rule feels made up.
misconception.why: Students sometimes doubt the unit's-digit rule because it isn't intuitive that squaring restricts the last digit.
misconception.remediationHint: Check a few squares yourself (3²=9, 13²=169, 23²=529) — none end in 3, and this holds for every perfect square.

questions.prompt: How many non-perfect-square numbers lie strictly between 12² and 13²?
hints: Between n² and (n+1)² there are always exactly 2n non-square numbers.
Here n = 12, so compute 2 × 12.

questions.prompt: Express 49 as the sum of consecutive odd numbers starting from 1. How many odd numbers did you need to add?
hints: Every perfect square n² is the sum of the first n odd numbers.
49 = 7², so how many odd numbers make up that sum?

questions.prompt: Is 40 a perfect square? Use the repeated-subtraction method (successively subtracting 1, 3, 5, ...) to decide.
hints: Keep subtracting consecutive odd numbers (1, then 3, then 5, ...) from 40.
If you land exactly on 0 at some step, it's a perfect square — if you go negative before that, it isn't.

questions.prompt: Using the form 2m, m²−1, m²+1, find the Pythagorean triplet whose smallest member is 10.
hints: Since 10 is the smallest member, try setting 2m = 10 and solve for m.
With m found, compute m² − 1 and m² + 1 to get the other two members.
List all three numbers in increasing order, separated by commas.

questions.prompt: Using the form 2m, m²−1, m²+1, find a Pythagorean triplet in which one member is 14.
hints: Try setting 2m = 14 first and see if m comes out to a whole number.
With m found, compute m² − 1 and m² + 1 to get the other two members.
List all three numbers in increasing order, separated by commas.

questions.prompt: Can a perfect square number end in exactly 3 zeros?
hints: Think about how many zeros a number's square gains compared to the number itself.
If a number ends in k zeros, its square ends in exactly 2k zeros — always an even count.

questions.prompt: What is the unit's digit of 78²?
hints: You only need the unit's digit of 78, not the whole number, to find the unit's digit of its square.
8 × 8 = 64 — what's the unit's digit of that?

questions.prompt: Using prime factorisation, is 180 a perfect square?
hints: Prime factorise 180 completely.
Check whether every prime factor can be grouped into a pair.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 180 must be multiplied to make it a perfect square.
hints: Prime factorise 180 and find which prime factor is left unpaired.
Multiplying by that unpaired factor completes the pair.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 200 must be divided to obtain a perfect square.
hints: Prime factorise 200 and find which prime factor appears an odd number of times.
Dividing out one copy of that factor leaves all factors paired.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest perfect square number that is divisible by each of 8, 12 and 18.
hints: First find the LCM of 8, 12 and 18.
Prime factorise the LCM and check whether every factor is already paired.
If any factor is unpaired, multiply the LCM by the missing partner to complete it.

questions.prompt: Find √196 using prime factorisation.
hints: Prime factorise 196 and pair up identical factors.
Multiply one factor from each pair together.

questions.prompt: Find √225 using prime factorisation.
hints: Prime factorise 225 and pair up identical factors.
Multiply one factor from each pair together.

questions.prompt: Using repeated subtraction of consecutive odd numbers, find √64.
hints: Subtract 1, then 3, then 5, and so on from 64, counting each subtraction.
Stop when you reach exactly 0 — the number of subtractions is the square root.

questions.prompt: Between which two consecutive whole numbers does √500 lie? Give the smaller one.
hints: Find two consecutive whole numbers whose squares fall just below and just above 500.
Try 22² and 23².

questions.prompt: The area of a square garden is 324 m². Find the length of its side.
hints: The side length of a square is the square root of its area.
Prime factorise 324 to find √324, and don't forget the unit.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
hints: Use the Pythagorean relation: hypotenuse² = leg² + leg².
Compute 9² + 12², then take the square root of the result.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest perfect square number that is divisible by 4, 9 and 25.
hints: First find the LCM of 4, 9 and 25.
Prime factorise the LCM and check whether every factor is already paired — if so, the LCM itself is your answer.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 1250 must be divided to obtain a perfect square.
hints: Prime factorise 1250 completely.
Find the prime factor that appears an odd number of times, and divide it out.

questions.prompt: What is √1?
hints: Which number multiplied by itself gives 1?

questions.prompt: Find √441.
hints: Prime factorise 441 and pair up identical factors.
Multiply one factor from each pair together.

questions.prompt: What is 6 cubed (6³)?
hints: Cubing a number means multiplying it by itself three times.
Compute 6 × 6 × 6.

questions.prompt: Is 100 a perfect cube?
hints: Think of the two consecutive whole numbers whose cubes fall just below and just above 100.
4³ = 64 and 5³ = 125 — does 100 match either one exactly?

questions.prompt: Which of these is a perfect cube: 125 or 150?
hints: Try cubing small whole numbers like 5 and see which one matches.

questions.prompt: Using prime factorisation, is 392 a perfect cube?
hints: Prime factorise 392 completely.
Check whether every prime factor can be grouped into a complete triple.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 392 must be multiplied to make it a perfect cube.
hints: Prime factorise 392 and find which prime factor's triple is incomplete.
Multiplying by the missing factor(s) completes that triple.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 250 must be divided to obtain a perfect cube.
hints: Prime factorise 250 and find which prime factor is left without a complete triple.
Dividing out that leftover factor leaves every remaining factor in a complete triple.

questions.prompt: The Hardy–Ramanujan number 1729 can be written as 1³ + 12³, or as the sum of two other cubes. Calculate 10³ + 9³ to find the second pair.
hints: Cube each number separately first: 10³ and 9³.
Then add the two results together.

questions.prompt: Find the cube of −4.
hints: Multiply −4 by itself three times, keeping track of the sign.
A negative number multiplied an odd number of times stays negative.

misconception.why: Students often assume cubing, like squaring, always produces a positive result.
misconception.remediationHint: Unlike squaring, cubing a negative number keeps it negative, because you're multiplying an odd number of negative signs together.

questions.prompt: What is the unit's digit of 12³?
hints: You only need the unit's digit of 12, not the whole number, to find the unit's digit of its cube.
2 × 2 × 2 = 8 — what's the unit's digit of that?

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 88 must be multiplied to make it a perfect cube.
hints: Prime factorise 88 completely — note how many times each prime factor appears.
One factor already appears in a complete triple; the other appears only once and needs two more copies to complete its triple.
Multiply by the square of that second factor to complete its triple.

questions.prompt: Find ∛8 (the cube root of 8).
hints: Which number, multiplied by itself three times, gives 8?

questions.prompt: Find ∛1000 (the cube root of 1000).
hints: Which number, multiplied by itself three times, gives 1000?

questions.prompt: Find the cube root of 3375 using prime factorisation.
hints: Prime factorise 3375 and group identical factors into triples.
Multiply one factor from each triple together.

questions.prompt: Find the cube root of 13824 using prime factorisation.
hints: Prime factorise 13824 and group identical factors into triples.
Multiply one factor from each triple together.

questions.prompt: A cube has a volume of 729 cm³. Find the length of its edge.
hints: The edge length of a cube is the cube root of its volume.
Prime factorise 729 to find ∛729, and don't forget the unit.

questions.prompt: Find the cube root of 74088 using prime factorisation.
hints: Prime factorise 74088 and group identical factors into triples.
Multiply one factor from each triple together.
You should find three distinct prime factors, each forming its own triple.

questions.prompt: Platform 2 on a control panel displays 295². Using the identity (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², find the value of 295² by writing 295 as (300 − 5).
hints: Set a = 300 and b = 5, since 295 = 300 − 5.
Compute a² − 2ab + b²: 300² − 2(300)(5) + 5².

misconception.why: Forgetting the middle term (−2ab) and computing only a² + b² (300² + 5²).
misconception.remediationHint: The identity has three terms, not two — always include −2ab between a² and b².

questions.prompt: Platform 1 on the same control panel displays 95². Using the same identity, find 95² by writing 95 as (100 − 5).
hints: Set a = 100 and b = 5, since 95 = 100 − 5.
Compute a² − 2ab + b²: 100² − 2(100)(5) + 5².

misconception.why: Forgetting the middle term (−2ab) and computing only a² + b² (100² + 5²).
misconception.remediationHint: The identity has three terms, not two — always include −2ab between a² and b².

questions.prompt: Platform 1 shows 95² and Platform 2 shows 295². Which platform's squared value is greater than 15,000?
hints: Compare each squared value to 15,000 directly.
95² is under 10,000; check where 295² lands.

misconception.why: Assuming any three-digit number squared automatically exceeds 15,000, without actually computing 95² first.
misconception.remediationHint: 95² is only 9,025 — always compute before comparing, rather than estimating from the size of the base number.

questions.prompt: Find √676.
hints: 26² = 676 — check by estimating between 25² = 625 and 30² = 900.
Try prime-factorising 676 and pairing identical factors.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 22² − 21² without squaring each number separately.
hints: Use the identity a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
Here a = 22 and b = 21, so (a − b) = 1.

questions.prompt: How many trailing zeros does 4,100² end in?
hints: Write 4,100 as 41 × 100, and square each part separately.
100² contributes four zeros; check whether 41² adds any more.

misconception.why: Assuming the zero count carries over unchanged from 4,100 itself instead of recomputing it for the squared value.
misconception.remediationHint: Squaring a number with trailing zeros doubles its trailing-zero count (100 has 2 zeros; 100² = 10,000 has 4).

questions.prompt: The sum 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 (the first five odd numbers) equals which of these?
hints: The sum of the first n odd numbers always equals n².
Count how many odd numbers are being added here.

misconception.why: Confusing this with the sum of the first 9 whole numbers (1+2+...+9=45) instead of adding the five odd numbers shown.
misconception.remediationHint: Add exactly the five numbers shown (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), not a different series.

questions.prompt: A treasure chest contains 5,400 identical golden coins. The total number of coins must be a perfect cube. Find the least number by which 5,400 should be divided so that the result is a perfect cube.
hints: Prime-factorise 5,400 and group the factors into triples.
One prime's power won't form a complete triple — that incomplete power is exactly what you need to remove.

misconception.why: Dividing by an unrelated factor instead of first prime-factorising fully and identifying the specific prime power that breaks the perfect-cube grouping.
misconception.remediationHint: 5,400 = 2³ × 3³ × 5² — only the 5² is an incomplete triple, so 25 (not any other factor) is what must go.

questions.prompt: Following the pattern 2³ = 8, 3³ = 27, 4³ = 64, find the next value: 5³.
hints: Multiply 5 × 5 × 5.
Each step in this pattern cubes the next whole number.

questions.prompt: A drone hovers such that its horizontal distance from a statue is 6 m, its height above the ground is 8 m, and the straight-line distance from the statue to the drone is 10 m. Do 6, 8 and 10 form a Pythagorean triplet?
hints: A Pythagorean triplet (a, b, c) satisfies a² + b² = c², where c is the largest number.
Check whether 6² + 8² equals 10².

misconception.why: Adding 6 + 8 + 10 or comparing the numbers directly instead of checking a² + b² = c².
misconception.remediationHint: You must square each number first, then add the two smaller squares and compare to the largest square.

questions.prompt: Given the pattern 4³ − 3³ = 1 + 4×3×3, 5³ − 4³ = 1 + 5×4×3, 6³ − 5³ = 1 + 6×5×3, use it to find the value of 9³ − 8³.
hints: Follow the same pattern with n = 9: 1 + 9×8×3.
Compute 9×8×3 first, then add 1.

questions.prompt: Using the same pattern, a student claims that 11³ − 10³ = 331. Is this claim correct?
hints: Apply the pattern with n = 11: 1 + 11×10×3.
Compare your computed value to 331.

misconception.why: Miscomputing 11×10×3 (a common multiplication slip) rather than an actual disagreement with the pattern.
misconception.remediationHint: 11×10=110, then 110×3=330, then +1=331 — the claim is correct.

questions.prompt: How many non-perfect-square numbers lie strictly between 20² and 21²?
hints: Between n² and (n+1)² there are always exactly 2n non-square numbers.
Here n = 20, so compute 2 × 20.

questions.prompt: Using repeated subtraction of consecutive odd numbers, find √81.
hints: Subtract 1, then 3, then 5, and so on from 81, counting each subtraction.
Stop when you reach exactly 0 — the number of subtractions is the square root.

questions.prompt: Between which two consecutive whole numbers does √150 lie? Give the smaller one.
hints: Find two consecutive whole numbers whose squares fall just below and just above 150.
Try 12² and 13².

questions.prompt: Between which two consecutive whole numbers does √300 lie? Give the smaller one.
hints: Find two consecutive whole numbers whose squares fall just below and just above 300.
Try 17² and 18².

questions.prompt: Which of these is the Pythagorean triplet formed using 2m, m²−1, m²+1 with m = 9?
hints: Compute 2m, m² − 1 and m² + 1 separately for m = 9.
m² = 81, so m² − 1 = 80 and m² + 1 = 82.

misconception.why: Forgetting to double m, using m itself instead of 2m as the first member of the triplet.
misconception.remediationHint: The first member of the triplet is 2m, not m — for m = 9, that's 18, not 9.

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped water tank has a volume of 2197 cm³. Find the length of its edge.
hints: The edge length of a cube is the cube root of its volume.
Prime factorise 2197 to find ∛2197, and don't forget the unit.

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number by which 1536 must be divided to make it a perfect cube.
hints: Prime factorise 1536 completely — note how many times each prime factor appears.
One factor already forms a complete triple (or triples); the other appears just once and breaks the grouping.
Dividing out that single leftover factor leaves every remaining factor in a complete triple.

questions.prompt: Can a perfect square number end in the digit 8?
hints: Recall which unit's digits are possible for a perfect square.
Perfect squares only ever end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
